aboutH2: Wilp Si’Satxw Community Healing Centre: First Nations Treatment in Kitwanga
intro: This rehabilitation centre is residential and has an approach that is holistic when it comes to treatment alcoholics and drug addicts. Its treatment will target four different aspects: the spiritual, emotional, mental, and physical sides of addiction. There is an individualized treatment for each patient based on exactly what they need to recover from their addiction. Then the program is made of individual and group counselling. There is also education involved and physical fitness. The program also offers psychological and professional help from trained individuals.

pillars.title: A Healing Centre on Cedarvale Road
pillars.body: The centre is on Cedarvale Road in Kitwanga, a small community in the Skeena region of Northern BC where Highway 37 leaves Highway 16, between Terrace and the Hazeltons. Clients live on site for the whole program. The kitchen staff cook the meals, a licensed practical nurse is part of the team, and the sweat lodge is used every week. The centre asks people to bring a sleeping bag, a pillow, three towels and clothes for the weather, for sweats and for exercise.

pillars.title: A Refresher Program Every January
pillars.body: Each year at Wilp Si’Satxw opens with a two-week Refresher program for former clients. People come back to pick up new tools, talk honestly about what went well and what didn't, and reconnect with other past clients and with staff. During treatment, workshops cover relapse prevention, goal setting and life skills. Alcoholics Anonymous and Narcotics Anonymous are part of the program too.

pillars.title: Counsellors, Elders and a Nurse
pillars.body: Executive Director Darlene Green has worked at the centre since 1996. She is a Certified Indigenous Addictions Specialist Level III and a chartered herbalist, and she leads sweats. Program Director Roy Davies first came to Wilp Si’Satxw as a client, went on to study at the Nicola Valley Institute of Technology and joined the staff in 2012. The treatment team also includes counsellors, a licensed practical nurse and a psychologist. An Elder advisor and client support workers work alongside them, and Elders from the Gitxsan Nations visit as guests.

overviewH2: Wilp Si’Satxw Community Healing Centre: Programs Overview
overview: Wilp Si’Satxw means "House of Purification". The centre is run by the Wilp Si’Satxw House of Purification Society, the name this listing used before, which was incorporated in April 1984 after a public meeting at Wrinch Memorial Hospital chose its first Board of Directors. In the society's words, its purpose is to provide a holistic, spiritually based Healing Centre where people can start on the road to recovery. It has been accredited by the Canadian Accreditation Council since 2003 and appears among the FNHA-funded treatment centres in the First Nations Health Authority's adult referral package.

afterOverview: Programs follow a fixed calendar. In 2026 the year started with the two-week Refresher in January, followed by a six-week Women's Wellness program, an eight-week Coed program, a seven-week IRS program, an eight-week 2 Spirit program and a six-week Men's Wellness program. The last Coed program of the year runs October 25 to December 17. Staff deliver the workshops using their formal training and their own lived experience, with a cultural approach where they can. Every program includes the weekly sweat lodge ceremony and drumming and singing, and clients are welcome to bring their own drums and songs.

location.heading: Wilp Si’Satxw Community Healing Centre in Kitwanga, British Columbia
location.intro: Wilp Si’Satxw is at 24 Cedarvale Road in Kitwanga, in the Skeena region of Northern BC, close to where Highway 37 meets Highway 16. By road it is about 15 hours from Vancouver, and flying to Terrace, then driving about 1 hour 15 minutes east, is the quicker option; the Hazeltons are about 40 minutes away, Smithers about 1 hour 30 minutes, Prince Rupert about 3 hours and Prince George about 5 hours 30 minutes.

faqIntro: Answers come from the centre's own website and public listings. Still unsure? Call, it's free and confidential.

faqs.q: How do I get into a program at Wilp Si’Satxw?
faqs.a: You need a referral. Alcohol and drug counsellors, band social workers, NNADAP workers, CHRs, other referral workers and any treatment or recovery centre can refer you. The referral worker fills in the assessment and referral package with you, and the complete application, including a pre-admission medical exam and a TB test, has to reach the centre before a treatment date is booked. Completed packages go to referrals@wilpchc.ca, and the centre books people in the order complete packages arrive.

faqs.q: How much does Wilp Si’Satxw cost?
faqs.a: The centre does not publish a fee. It is run by a non-profit society and is listed among the FNHA-funded First Nations treatment centres in the First Nations Health Authority's adult referral package. Your referral worker or the centre's office can tell you how your stay and travel would be covered.

faqs.q: How long are the programs, and when do they start?
faqs.a: Programs run 2, 6, 7 or 8 weeks. The current 8-week Coed program runs October 25 to December 17, 2026. The 2027 calendar opens with the 2-week Refresher (January 10 to 21), then the 6-week Women's Wellness program (January 24 to March 4) and an 8-week Coed program (March 7 to April 29). The first day starts at 8:00 am and the last day ends at 2:00 pm.

No. You must have two weeks of full sobriety before treatment, with no alcohol and no psychoactive medications or drugs, so withdrawal has to be handled before you arrive. Talk to your referral worker about detox options closer to home.

faqs.q: Can I attend if I take methadone or Suboxone?
faqs.a: Yes, if your dose is stable. The centre asks for 2 months on the same Suboxone dose or 4 months on the same methadone dose, and the dose will not change while you are there. The daily dose cannot be more than 20 mg of Suboxone or 70 mg of methadone, Kadian is not accepted at this time, and each program takes up to 2 OAT clients.

It is a seven-week program for survivors of Indian Residential School, Day School and the Sixties Scoop, and for their children and the generations after them. Workshops use a cultural lens where possible and focus on breaking the cycle of alcohol and drug abuse by understanding generational trauma, behaviour patterns and triggers. In 2026 it ran May 10 to June 25.

faqs.q: Where is Wilp Si’Satxw and how do I get there?
faqs.a: The centre is at 24 Cedarvale Road in Kitwanga, in Northern BC. Terrace is about 1 hour 15 minutes away by car and has the nearest major airport, and the Hazeltons are about 40 minutes away. From Vancouver it is roughly 15 hours by road.

Bring comfortable clothing for the weather, sweats and exercise, plus personal hygiene items. The centre also asks for a sleeping bag, a pillow and three towels, a phone or calling card, laundry soap and dryer sheets, and paper and stamps for writing.

faqs.q: What happens after my program ends?
faqs.a: Former clients can return for the two-week Refresher program held at the start of each year. It is a chance to learn new tools, share what has worked and what hasn't, and lean on a network of past clients and Wilp Si’Satxw staff. AA and NA meetings are also part of the program itself.

Yes. The centre has been accredited by the Canadian Accreditation Council since 2003. The Wilp Si’Satxw House of Purification Society that runs it was incorporated in British Columbia on April 13, 1984.

faqs.q: How do I contact the centre?
faqs.a: Call 250-849-5211 or toll free 1-877-849-5211, Monday to Friday from 8:30 am to 4:30 pm. You can also email info@wilpchc.ca, or fax 250-849-5374. The mailing address is Box 429, Cedarvale Road, Kitwanga, BC V0J 2A0.
